<document>
# Reduced Working Time and Productivity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

*Review of Work and Employment Research. S. Achterberg, N. Iwu, F. Castell and J. Moreno. Review protocol registered before search.*

## Abstract

We systematically reviewed studies of reductions in scheduled working time of at least 10% with pay maintained, reporting a quantitative measure of output. Twenty-three studies (1998–2025; about 41,000 workers) met inclusion criteria. Pooled across studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0), with very high heterogeneity (I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4). Study design, the hours measure and the type of work explain much of the heterogeneity: controlled studies found smaller effects (+8.2%) than uncontrolled before–after studies (+18.7%), studies using actual hours found smaller effects (+7.9%) than those using scheduled hours (+16.6%), and per-worker output fell substantially in coverage-bound work (−8.9%) but not in discretionary work (+0.6%). There is evidence of small-study bias; adjusting for it reduces the pooled per-hour estimate to +9.1%. Effects show no sign of decay over time.

## Methods

**Search and inclusion.** We searched four bibliographic databases and two working-paper repositories, and contacted authors of known pilots. Studies were included if they (a) evaluated a reduction in scheduled hours of at least 10% with no reduction in pay; (b) reported output per worker or output per hour, or data from which either could be derived; and (c) had at least 50 workers. We excluded studies reporting only self-rated productivity. Of 412 records screened, 23 studies met the criteria.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome is the change in output per hour, expressed as a log ratio and converted back to a percentage for reporting. Where a study reported both scheduled and actual hours, we used actual hours. The secondary outcome is the change in output per worker. For controlled studies we used the difference relative to the comparison group; for uncontrolled studies, the change from baseline.

**Coding of work type.** Two coders independently classified each study's setting as *discretionary* (output can be produced at any time within a deadline: case processing, professional services, software, back-office work), *coverage-bound* (output depends on staff being present while demand arrives: counters, contact centres, retail floors, care rotas), or *mixed/unclear*. Agreement was high (κ = 0.84); disagreements were resolved by discussion.

**Synthesis.** Random-effects meta-analysis with restricted maximum-likelihood estimation; moderators examined by meta-regression. Small-study effects assessed by funnel plot, Egger's regression test, and trim-and-fill.

## Included studies

Of the 23 studies, 9 had a comparison group (3 randomised, including the Varden County trial; 6 matched or difference-in-differences) and 14 were uncontrolled before–after designs, including the Halden multi-organisation pilot. Eight studies measured actual hours; 15 used scheduled hours only. Thirteen settings were coded discretionary, 7 coverage-bound and 3 mixed or unclear. Only two studies were in manufacturing, both in the mixed category. Follow-up ranged from 3 to 30 months (median 6). Output measures were record-based in 12 studies and manager-reported in 11.

## Results

### Pooled effects

Across all 23 studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0; I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4; I² = 74%). The prediction interval for output per hour runs from −4% to +34%, meaning that a new study in an unknown setting could plausibly find anything from a small loss to a very large gain.

### Moderators

**Table 1. Subgroup estimates of the change in output per hour and output per worker**

| Subgroup | k | Output per hour | Output per worker |
|---|---|---|---|
| **All studies** | 23 | +13.4% (8.1 to 19.0) | −1.8% (−4.9 to +1.4) |
| Controlled designs | 9 | +8.2% (4.0 to 12.6) | −4.1% (−7.6 to −0.5) |
| Uncontrolled before–after | 14 | +18.7% (11.2 to 26.7) | −0.2% (−4.0 to +3.8) |
| Actual hours measured | 8 | +7.9% (3.6 to 12.4) | −3.9% (−7.8 to +0.1) |
| Scheduled hours only | 15 | +16.6% (9.9 to 23.7) | −0.6% (−4.3 to +3.3) |
| Record-based output | 12 | +9.7% (5.0 to 14.6) | −3.6% (−7.2 to +0.2) |
| Manager-reported output | 11 | +17.8% (10.0 to 26.1) | +0.4% (−3.9 to +4.9) |
| Discretionary work | 13 | +15.1% (8.8 to 21.8) | +0.6% (−2.8 to +4.1) |
| Coverage-bound work | 7 | +6.2% (1.1 to 11.6) | −8.9% (−13.1 to −4.5) |
| Mixed or unclear | 3 | +12.0% (−1.5 to 27.4) | −2.9% (−10.6 to +5.4) |

In a multiple meta-regression including design, hours measure and work type together, all three moderators remained associated with the effect, and together they explained 58% of between-study variance. The design and measurement moderators overlap heavily: 12 of the 14 uncontrolled studies used scheduled hours, and 9 of the 14 used manager-reported output. Our data cannot fully separate them.

The work-type moderator is the clearest for the per-worker outcome. In discretionary work, output per worker was essentially unchanged in pooled estimates; in coverage-bound work, it fell by about 9%, consistent across all seven studies (I² = 22%). The per-hour gain in coverage-bound work was real but too small to compensate for the hours lost.

Note that the discretionary estimate of +15.1% per hour mixes controlled and uncontrolled studies. Restricting to the five controlled discretionary studies, the per-hour estimate is +9.6% (4.8 to 14.6) and the per-worker estimate −2.7% (−6.5 to +1.2).

### Small-study effects

The funnel plot is asymmetric, with small studies reporting larger per-hour gains (Egger's test p = 0.02). Trim-and-fill imputes five missing studies on the left of the funnel and reduces the pooled per-hour estimate from +13.4% to +9.1% (95% CI 3.9 to 14.6). We interpret this as evidence that small, favourable pilots are more likely to be published or publicised than small, unfavourable ones.

### Duration

Four studies reported follow-up beyond 12 months. Their pooled per-hour gain was +14.0% (95% CI 6.2 to 22.4), indistinguishable from the overall estimate. Effects show no sign of decay, and novelty explanations can therefore be set aside.

### Mechanisms

Eleven studies measured fatigue or wellbeing alongside output. Across these, the study-level correlation between the improvement in fatigue scores and the per-hour gain was weak (r = 0.18). Only three studies measured time spent in meetings, and none tested meetings as a mediator under a registered plan; we cannot assess this mechanism. Sick leave fell in all 14 studies that reported it (pooled −31%), and staff turnover fell in all 9 that reported it.

## Discussion

The literature supports a gain in output per hour from reduced working time, but a considerably smaller one than headline pilots suggest. The figure most often quoted, a gain of more than 20%, comes from uncontrolled studies using scheduled hours and manager-reported output; each of those features is associated with larger estimates. Controlled studies, studies measuring actual hours, studies using records, and the bias-adjusted estimate converge on a gain of roughly 8 to 10%.

Whether that gain is "enough" depends on the type of work. In discretionary settings the evidence is compatible with output per worker being maintained or falling slightly; in coverage-bound settings it falls clearly, and maintaining service would require additional staff.

We do not find support for the claim, made in one re-analysis of the Halden pilot, that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact. The controlled and actual-hours subgroups, which avoid the problems that re-analysis identified, still show gains whose confidence intervals exclude zero. Nor do we find support for the claim that reduced hours are sector-general.

## Limitations

Twenty-three studies is a small base for a meta-regression with three correlated moderators. Most studies are short. Only nine are controlled, and the controlled studies are themselves mostly in the public sector. Manufacturing and shift-based production are almost absent. Classification of work type, though reliable between coders, imposes a binary on what is often a mix within a single organisation.

response:
This is the most balanced of the four documents. It pools all the evidence and arrives at a position between the Halden pilot's ">20%, sector-general" and Varga and Holm's "entirely an artifact": a per-hour gain of roughly 8–10%, with output per worker falling clearly in coverage-bound work. That conclusion fits what the earlier documents jointly suggested. The numbers are internally consistent. The main weaknesses are four:

- The claim that effects don't decay rests on far too little.
- Small-study bias is hard to separate from differences in study design.
- The "convergence" on 8–10% comes from overlapping groups of studies, not independent lines of evidence.
- Studies that mix several kinds of work, such as Halden and Varden, are coded as a single unit.

## 1. The numbers are internally consistent

- **Counts.** Every split adds to 23: 9 controlled + 14 uncontrolled; 8 actual hours + 15 scheduled; 12 record-based + 11 manager-reported; 13 discretionary + 7 coverage-bound + 3 mixed.
- **Confidence intervals.** Every interval I checked is symmetric on the log scale around its point estimate, as it should be when pooling log ratios. That includes the overall estimates, all ten subgroup rows, trim-and-fill, the duration subgroup and the controlled-discretionary restriction.
- **Prediction interval.** The −4% to +34% interval implies between-study SD τ ≈ 0.076 on the log scale and a typical within-study standard error of about 0.037. Both are plausible given I² = 81%.
- **Per-hour and per-worker rows agree.** Dividing per-worker by per-hour gives the implied cut in hours:

| Subgroup | Implied hours cut |
|---|---|
| Actual hours measured | about 11% |
| Scheduled hours only | about 15% |
| Controlled designs | about 11% |
| Coverage-bound work | about 14% |

These are plausible given an inclusion threshold of a 10% scheduled cut, Halden's 14% actual cut and Varden's 13–17%.

## 2. The duration claim is the weakest conclusion

The abstract says "Effects show no sign of decay," and the results say novelty "can therefore be set aside." Both rest on four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, compared against all the others. The problems:

- **It compares studies, not time points.** Decay should be tested within studies, by following each study's effect from early to late follow-up. Comparing long studies with short ones mixes duration with every other way the studies differ.
- **No adjustment for design.** If the four long studies are mostly uncontrolled, the right comparison is the uncontrolled subgroup (+18.7%). Against that, their +14.0% would hint at decay, not rule it out.
- **Selection on survival.** Schemes that are still running and being evaluated after a year are mostly ones that worked. Halden's own reversions and withdrawals show that failing schemes drop out early.
- **The interval is too wide to rule out decay.** A CI of 6.2% to 22.4% is compatible with substantial decay. With four studies, a Hartung–Knapp interval using t on 3 degrees of freedom would be wider still.

A defensible version would be: "The few longer studies do not suggest strong decay, but the evidence cannot exclude it."

## 3. Small-study bias can't be separated from study design

The funnel asymmetry may not reflect publication bias. In this literature, the smallest studies are typically uncontrolled pilots with scheduled hours and manager-reported output, the three features the review itself links to larger effects. With I² = 81% and strong moderators, Egger's test and trim-and-fill are known to give misleading results, because real differences between studies look like missing studies.

The review should:

- run Egger's test inside the moderator meta-regression, adding the standard error alongside design, hours measure and work type;
- check whether asymmetry remains within the controlled studies alone;
- present the 9.1% as one possible adjustment, not as evidence that "small, favourable pilots are more likely to be published."

This matters for the Discussion. The bias-adjusted figure and the design subgroups are driven by the same small uncontrolled studies, so they are not independent confirmations of each other.

## 4. "Convergence on 8–10%" uses overlapping groups of studies

The Discussion cites four estimates as if they were independent:

| Estimate | Gain per hour |
|---|---|
| Controlled designs | 8.2% |
| Actual hours measured | 7.9% |
| Record-based output | 9.7% |
| Bias-adjusted (trim-and-fill) | 9.1% |

These groups overlap heavily. From the counts given, 6 of the 9 controlled studies used actual hours and 7 used record-based output. Each subgroup also still includes the other biases; for example, 3 controlled studies used scheduled hours.

The more convincing analysis is a best-evidence estimate. Pool the studies that are controlled, measure actual hours and use record-based output together, and pool the three randomised trials on their own. Varden's case-processing stratum (+12.5%, CI +6.9 to +18.4) would be one of them. If that subset also lands around 8–10%, the conclusion is much stronger. If it has only two or three studies, say so.

A formal risk-of-bias assessment (for example ROBINS-I, with RoB 2 for the randomised trials) and a GRADE certainty rating would also be expected in a systematic review. The moderator analysis partly substitutes for them, but not fully.

## 5. Studies that mix types of work are coded as one unit

- **Halden** covers six sectors, including retail and hospitality, yet it receives one work-type code. If it is coded discretionary, its weak retail results are hidden in the discretionary pool. Halden reports sector-level results, so these should be extracted separately.
- **Varden** randomised within strata and reports separate results for case-processing (discretionary) and counter work (coverage-bound). It must either appear as two entries or be coded "mixed." The review should say which. If it appears twice, the count of 23 and the 3 randomised trials need clarifying.
- **Halden's figures.** It should state which version of Halden was used:
  - Halden reported only scheduled hours and manager-reported output, and had non-random attrition.
  - Varga and Holm's reanalysis gives actual hours and record-based output for subsets of organisations.
  - The review's rule of using actual hours where available implies it should use the corrected figures, or at least test them in a sensitivity analysis. The reanalysis must not be counted as a separate study.

The Limitations section acknowledges that coding imposes a binary. The bigger problem is that whole studies are coded as one unit when sector- or stratum-level results are available.

## 6. Rebuttal of the "entirely an artifact" claim

The conclusion is right, but the argument has a gap. Varga and Holm named three problems: measurement, selection and novelty.

- **Measurement.** The actual-hours and record-based subgroups address this. ✓
- **Selection.** Only the 3 randomised trials remove it. Matched and difference-in-differences studies still involve organisations choosing whether to adopt, so "controlled" is weaker protection than the Discussion implies.
- **Novelty.** This is addressed only by the duration analysis in section 2, which can't bear the weight.

The rebuttal would be strongest using the randomised trials, and in particular Varden, which avoids selection and measurement problems and held its result over nine months.

## 7. Calling the per-hour gain in coverage-bound work "real"

The coverage-bound per-hour gain (+6.2%) is described as "real but too small to compensate." As I noted for Varden, when demand arrives on its own schedule and fewer staff are present, staff spend less time idle between customers. Part of that per-hour gain is therefore higher utilisation, with the cost borne by the public through longer waits. The review should say it may partly reflect queueing rather than staff working more effectively, and report waiting times or service-level measures where the studies have them.

## 8. Smaller points

- **Mechanisms.** The study-level correlation between fatigue improvement and per-hour gain (r = 0.18, k = 11) is not evidence of a weak link. Its 95% CI runs from about −0.47 to +0.70. Correlations across studies are also a poor test of mechanisms within organisations. "Uninformative" fits better than "weak."
- **Sick leave and turnover.** "Fell in all 14 / all 9 studies" counts studies rather than pooling effects, and is exposed to selective reporting, since studies tend to report wellbeing outcomes when they look good. A pooled estimate with an interval, split by design, would be better.
- **Low I² in coverage-bound work.** I² = 22% does not show the effect was "consistent across all seven studies." Report whether all seven point estimates were negative.
- **Moderator model.** Three correlated moderators across 23 studies risks overfitting. Report the coefficients with Knapp–Hartung intervals, and a model with an interaction or a single combined risk-of-bias score.
- **Manager-reported output.** It is included, while self-rated productivity is excluded. Given Varga and Holm's finding of a gap of about 4 points against records, a sensitivity analysis excluding manager-reported studies should be reported.
- **Pre-specification.** The protocol was registered before the search. The review should state which subgroups were pre-specified. The duration analysis and the controlled-discretionary restriction look post hoc.
- **Search.** Contacting authors of "known pilots" favours well-publicised schemes, a further possible source of small-study bias worth noting.

## 9. Conclusion supported by the evidence

> Reduced working time at full pay is associated with a gain in output per hour of roughly 8–10% in better-designed studies, smaller than headline pilots report but unlikely to be zero. In discretionary work, output per worker is approximately maintained or falls slightly. In coverage-bound work, it falls by about 9% and service suffers unless staff are added. Most studies are short, and evidence on whether gains persist beyond a year is too thin to rule out decay.

Across all four documents, the best-supported position is close to this. Per-hour gains are real but modest, they depend heavily on how hours and output are measured, and the policy question turns on whether output depends on staff being present.

I can draft a referee report on this review, or write a synthesis of all four documents.
